content: The Review Manager (RevMan) file was obtained from the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group and was tailored to focus on the key comparisons and outcomes relevant to the guideline, excluding irrelevant data. This customized file was then exported to the GRADE profiler software (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation), where the GRADE criteria were applied to critically appraise the retrieved scientific evidence. Evidence profiles, presented as GRADE tables, were subsequently prepared for each comparison. This process was conducted collaboratively online between the WHO Guideline Steering Group and an external team of guideline methodologists. The evidence summarized in the GRADE tables was derived from a substantial body of data, primarily extracted from Cochrane reviews, many of which included multiple comparisons. Each GRADE table corresponded to a specific question or comparison, although some tables lacked data for all critical outcomes due to the unavailability of such data in the Cochrane reviews. The raw data used to construct the GRADE tables are not included in this document but can be made available to interested readers. The Guideline Steering Group used the information in the GRADE tables to draft recommendations for each question. These recommendations were organized into thematic modules, which included narrative summaries of evidence and the relevant GRADE tables. The standardized criteria for grading evidence and the thematic modules (including the GRADE tables) are published separately in a document titled WHO Recommendations for Augmentation of Labour: Evidence Base. An initial online consultation was conducted to review the draft recommendations. The draft recommendations and supporting evidence were shared with members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG), who were invited to provide comments on the document in tracked mode. Members of the GDG and additional experts from WHO regional offices were then invited to attend the WHO technical consultation on augmentation of labour, held at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, on 26–27 September 2013. Participants were provided with the draft recommendations, narrative evidence summaries, GRADE tables, and other related documents in advance of the meeting. During the technical consultation, the values, preferences, and judgments regarding the strength of the recommendations were summarized. Participants were required to declare any relevant interests before the meeting, in accordance with WHO regulations. All GDG members and other participants completed a Declaration of Interest form, which was reviewed by the Guideline Steering Group prior to finalizing invitations. At the start of the meeting, GDG members were also asked to verbally declare any potential conflicts of interest. The management of conflicts of interest followed WHO guidelines, and all GDG members declared that they had no academic, commercial, or financial interests directly or indirectly related to the subject of the meeting. The decision-making process during the technical consultation was guided by a protocol that allowed participants to discuss and revise each draft recommendation as necessary. Final adoption of each recommendation was achieved by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of the participants, provided that those who disagreed did not feel strongly about their position. Strong disagreements would have been noted in the final guideline if they had occurred. In cases where consensus could not be reached, the disputed recommendation or decision was put to a vote, requiring a simple majority for approval unless the disagreement involved a safety concern. WHO staff, external methodologists, and observers at the meeting were not eligible to vote. The strength of each recommendation was initially aligned with the quality of the evidence, with strong recommendations based on moderate or high-quality evidence and weak recommendations based on low or very low-quality evidence. Additional factors considered in determining the strength and direction of the recommendations included values and preferences, the magnitude of effect, the balance of benefits versus harms, resource use, and feasibility. These considerations were documented using balance worksheets, which also recorded the reasons for any changes made to the default strength of the recommendations. The Guideline Steering Group prepared a preliminary version of the guideline document using a reporting template developed as part of WHO’s GREAT project. This draft was shared with invited participants one week before the meeting for their comments. During the meeting, the draft recommendations were modified based on participants’ deliberations and feedback from the preliminary online consultation. After the meeting, the Guideline Steering Group revised the document to accurately reflect the discussions and decisions of the participants. The revised draft was sent to the External Review Group for their input, which was carefully evaluated for inclusion in the final document. No substantive changes to the scope or recommendations of the guideline were made after the technical consultation. Stakeholders from all WHO regions participated in a preliminary online survey, and their feedback was used to refine the recommendation questions and prioritize outcomes. Annex 2 of the guideline lists the maternal and infant outcomes rated as “critical” and “important” by survey participants. A total of 27 Cochrane systematic reviews, summarized in 82 GRADE tables, provided the evidence base for the 20 recommendations included in the guideline. These recommendations were finalized during the WHO technical consultation. The recommendations address prioritized questions related to the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of delays in the first stage of labour, as well as supportive care for women undergoing labour augmentation. The recommendations on diagnosis and prevention focus on methods to assess labour progress and intrapartum interventions to prevent delays and avoid the need for augmentation. Recommendations on treatment address pharmacological and non-pharmacological methods of labour augmentation.
